cur:catacombs-arles-nativity.summary: Two fields of wavy strigils frame a central panel in two tiers showing the Nativity, with further figures at the corners. The rippling strigils, a decoration inherited from pagan sarcophagi, give way at the centre to the birth of Christ.
facts: The museum states that it is carved from marble of Saint-Béat in the Pyrenees and dates from the end of the 4th century.
Its use of Pyrenean marble points to a regional workshop rather than an import from Rome.

cur:catacombs-astorga-sarcophagus.summary: A continuous frieze of short, sturdy figures shows biblical scenes, with Christ healing and working miracles among the apostles and other figures. Imported from Rome, it shows how early Christian sarcophagi reached the far northwest of the Iberian Peninsula.
facts: The museum dates it to about 310 and states that it comes from Astorga cathedral; Commons associates it with San Justo de la Vega (León).
It is catalogued in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional as inv. 50310.

cur:manuscripts-sacramentary-charles-bal.summary: Christ sits within a blue and green mandorla, holding a book and raising in his right hand a small white disc — the eucharistic host — while two flaming seraphim flank him. Below, the reclining personifications of Earth and Ocean look up, and the text of the Sanctus ('Holy, holy, holy Lord God of hosts') in gold letters on purple fills the bottom of the page. The image places the heavenly song of the angels at the heart of the Mass.
facts: Only an unfinished fragment of ten leaves survives, but it has two initial pages and five full-page miniatures; it entered the royal library in Paris in 1732 from the estate of Jean-Baptiste Colbert.
The manuscript is attributed to the court school of Charles the Bald, whose location after the destruction of Saint-Martin at Tours in 853 is disputed.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, with a cross-nimbus and holding a red book, sits in a green mandorla carried by angels, while below him armed men and fallen figures struggle on the ground. The verse above speaks of God who 'subdueth the people under me' (Vulgate Psalm 17:48).
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-82-christ.summary: With his back to us, the psalmist entreats the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who holds spear, shield and scroll between two angels, to act against the nations that have taken counsel together. Angels in the heavens hurl firebrands, 'as the fire burneth a wood', at mounted hosts blowing trumpets across the foreground. The lower drawing of folio 48v is among the most turbulent battle scenes in the book.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-82-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-103-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, blessing and holding a book, walks upon the personified winds — 'who walketh upon the wings of the wind' — with two angels approaching as his ministers, and the moon and setting sun beside him. Below unfolds the creation praised in the psalm, beginning with the valleys, mountains and springs and the creatures that live among them. It is a panorama of Christ as Creator.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-103-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-christ-before-.summary: Above, Christ stands bound among soldiers in the hall of the high priest, who sits enthroned at the right, while at the door Peter warms himself by the fire and is questioned by the maid. Below, Christ is led before the seated high priest, who points his staff at him. The cock perched on the roof marks the moment of Peter's denial.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-christ-before-.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 497); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-castelseprio-presentation.summary: Before a canopy on columns, the aged Simeon bends forward with veiled hands to receive the Christ Child, whom the haloed Virgin holds out to him across the altar. The figure of Simeon, with his white beard and stooping posture, is one of the most admired passages of the Castelseprio cycle.
facts: The frescoes of Santa Maria foris portas were rediscovered under later plaster only in 1944; their date and the origin of their painter remain controversial, though the first half of the 9th century is increasingly favoured.
They show strong Byzantine influence combined with a freedom of handling recalling late antique painting, and are often described as the finest early medieval pictorial cycle in Italy.
Much of the painted surface was pitted to key the later plaster that covered it, damage that is especially visible in the Presentation scene.

vam:O88285.summary: Carved in high relief, Christ hangs on the cross beneath a titulus naming him Jesus of Nazareth, King, with the Sun and Moon above and an angel bowing towards him. At the left the Virgin stands with Ecclesia, who holds up a cup to catch his blood; at the right St John and the haloed Synagoga turn away with her banner. Below, Longinus and Stephaton flank the cross, the dead look out from their tombs, and Earth with her serpent and Sea on a sea-horse watch from the lowest corners. The plaque, now split, gathers heaven, earth and sea, Church and Synagogue around the cross in one great theological image.
facts: The titulus reads IHS NAZA / RENVS RE(X).

The V&A suggests that the plaque comes from a cover of the Gandersheim Gospels, written at Metz under Bishop Adventius (858–875); the other cover, with the Resurrection, remains with the manuscript at the Veste Coburg.
Its iconography is close to the V&A's Crucifixion ivory 250-1867, part of a group of Metz ivories of the third quarter of the 9th century.
vam:O88285.notes: Metz, ca. 860 (V&A). The link with the Gandersheim Gospels is given as 'probably'. Formerly in the Webb collection.

wga:zearly/1/1sculptu/sarcopha/1/7passio.summary: Twisted columns divide the front of this sarcophagus into five scenes of the Passion, told as a triumph. At the left Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; next a soldier sets a wreath, not a crown of thorns, on the head of the young Christ; at the right Christ is led before Pilate, who sits in thought as a servant brings water to wash his hands. In the centre, the cross is crowned by the chi-rho in a victor's wreath, with doves on its arms and two stunned soldiers below: the Resurrection shown not as a scene but as a sign of victory.
facts: The Vatican Museums record that it comes from the cemetery of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina and date it to about 350 (inv. 31525).
The museum interprets the crowning with thorns as transformed into a crowning with a jewelled diadem, so that the Passion is shown as glorious.
No crucified Christ appears: in the mid-4th century the cross with the chi-rho stood for the Resurrection (Anastasis), while the stunned soldiers allude to the guards at the tomb.
wga:zearly/1/1sculptu/sarcopha/1/7passio.notes: Commonly known as the 'Passion sarcophagus' (formerly Lateran 171).

feat:gill-westminster-stations-trial-pan.summary: This carved panel is Eric Gill's trial piece for the fourteen Stations of the Cross he made for Westminster Cathedral in London between 1914 and 1918. Christ, bowed under the cross, is helped by Simon of Cyrene, and both figures are cut in shallow, linear relief with the sacred words carved in Gill's own lettering. Its simple, almost archaic clarity broke with Victorian devotional sentiment and helped shape a new, modern language for church art in Britain.
facts: Gill was a surprising choice for the Westminster commission, which he received in 1914: he had become a Catholic only the year before, had been working as a sculptor for just three years, and was better known as a letter-cutter.
The inscriptions are integral to the design: Gill was one of the great letterers of the century and later designed the Gill Sans and Perpetua typefaces.

The finished Stations remain on the piers of Westminster Cathedral. Gill's reputation was reassessed after Fiona MacCarthy's 1989 biography revealed the sexual abuse recorded in his diaries; in 1998 a survivors' group called for the Stations to be removed, but the cathedral has kept them.
